note: One expectation index per contract directory. Each case names the structural violations that prove its point as (pointer, keyword) pairs; a validator's free-text message is deliberately never recorded. The expected set must be a subset of what the validator reports, because a conditional rule often reports a broader violation alongside the specific one.

status-pending.proves: There is no PENDING status. A record is written when a stage begins, so a pre-start status would say the same thing as the absence of the record — and the superseded model asserted both at once.

status-queued.proves: QUEUED is a global run state, not a stage status. Borrowing it here would start the drift towards one shared vocabulary and, from there, towards projecting one onto the other.

status-unknown.proves: The stage status vocabulary is closed at four values, unlike stage_id, whose vocabulary is deliberately open. Openness is a per-member decision, not a property of the contract.

status-lowercase.proves: The status vocabulary is case-sensitive, so a lowercased token cannot be matched against an approved status by accident.

stage-id-lowercase.proves: An open vocabulary is not a free-text member: stage_id still has a lexical shape, so any stage a later slice introduces is a stable upper-snake token rather than prose.

run-state-property.proves: A stage record carries no global run state. Carrying one would make every writer of a stage record decide a global fact, which is the projection this slice refuses to build.

terminal-without-finished-at.proves: A stage that reached a terminal status states when it ended, by the same rule the run state document applies to itself.

running-with-finished-at.proves: The converse: a stage still running has no end instant, so finished_at is refused rather than tolerated.
